claim: The Activator Protein 1 (AP-1) site (TGANTCA), a consensus sequence for the FOS/JUN family transcription factors, was identified as the most highly enriched motif among 11,830 previously identified neuronal activity-regulated enhancers.
source: The Activator Protein 1 (AP-1) site (TGANTCA), a consensus sequence for the FOS/JUN family transcription factors, was initially identified as the most highly enriched motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from screening 11,830 activity-regulated enhancers and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple transcription factors often bind enhancers co-operatively or competitively to tightly regulate gene expression in a combinatorial manner.
source: We further considered that multiple transcription factors often bind enhancers co-operatively or competitively to tightly regulate gene expression in a combinatorial manner (Hermsen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hermsen et al., 2006.

claim: The core NRE/AP-1 DNA motifs were inserted into the central midline element (CME), resulting in a 24 bp 'enhancer module.'
source: We inserted the core NRE/AP-1 DNA motifs into the central midline element (CME), a characterized transcriptional regulatory sequence whose secondary structure is favorable for transcription activation (Wharton et al., 1994), resulting in a 24 bp 'enhancer module.'
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and construction of the enhancer module, with citation to Wharton et al., 1994 for the CME properties.

claim: The synthetic promoter PRAM consists of four tandem repeats of an enhancer module upstream of the human FOS minimal promoter, resulting in a 199 bp synthetic promoter.
source: Unless otherwise stated, we assembled promoters by placing four tandem repeats of an enhancer module upstream of the human FOS minimal promoter, resulting in a 199 bp synthetic promoter (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim describes the construction of PRAM and is illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: When the NRE and AP-1 motifs partially overlapped by two base-pairs to form a 10mer TCGTGANTCA, the resulting synthetic promoter had the strongest activity-dependent induction profile.
source: The relative position of the NRE and AP-1 sites turned out to be critical. When these motifs partially overlapped by two base-pairs to form a 10mer TCGTGANTCA, the resulting synthetic promoter had the strongest activity-dependent induction profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The CME alone was not responsive to neuronal activity.
source: The CME alone was not responsive to activity (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: PRAM performance was not improved by replacing the NRE/AP-1 element with other highly enriched AP-1 containing 10mers found in the 11,830 neuronal activity-regulated enhancers.
source: Furthermore, PRAM performance was not improved by replacing the NRE/AP-1 element with other highly enriched AP-1 containing 10mers found in the 11,830 neuronal activity-regulated enhancers, indicating the significance of the NRE and AP-1 combination in our design (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: There was no correlation between 10mer enrichment and fold induction in the luciferase assay.
source: In general, we found no correlation between 10mer enrichment and fold induction in the luciferase assay (Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Removing or substituting the minimal promoter substantially reduced the fold induction of PRAM.
source: We proceeded with further characterization of PRAM and found that removing or substituting the minimal promoter (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), or changing the number of enhancer modules substantially reduced the fold induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2c,d.

claim: Changing the number of enhancer modules substantially reduced the fold induction of PRAM.
source: We proceeded with further characterization of PRAM and found that removing or substituting the minimal promoter (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), or changing the number of enhancer modules substantially reduced the fold induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: PRAM had among the highest fold induction when compared to several other activity-regulated promoters.
source: When compared to several other activity-regulated promoters, PRAM had among the highest fold induction (Figure 1c) and the highest relative luciferase activity in response to neuronal stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PRAM had the highest relative luciferase activity in response to neuronal stimulation compared to several other activity-regulated promoters.
source: When compared to several other activity-regulated promoters, PRAM had among the highest fold induction (Figure 1c) and the highest relative luciferase activity in response to neuronal stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: ESARE had a significantly lower fold induction than PRAM, due to its high basal activity.
source: We compared PRAM to another recently developed synthetic activity-dependent promoter, ESARE, which was based on the promoter of the IEG Arc (Kawashima et al., 2013). ESARE had a significantly lower fold induction, due to its high basal activity (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative experimental data shown in Figure 1d and cites Kawashima et al., 2013.

claim: PRAM has the largest fold induction of any activity-dependent promoter small enough to be packaged into an AAV.
source: Notably, PRAM has by far the largest fold induction of any activity-dependent promoter small enough to be packaged into an AAV.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with other promoters and the size constraint of AAV packaging.

claim: Over-expression of FOS, NPAS4, or both proteins in combination was sufficient to drive transcription through PRAM.
source: We next verified that PRAM has the characteristics expected from the presence of the FOS and NPAS4 binding motifs. Indeed, over-expression of FOS, NPAS4, or both proteins in combination was sufficient to drive transcription through PRAM (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Expression from PRAM was strongly induced by Ca2+ influx.
source: Indeed, over-expression of FOS, NPAS4, or both proteins in combination was sufficient to drive transcription through PRAM (Figure 1e). Expression from PRAM was strongly induced by Ca2+ influx (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b) and by various growth factors known to induce Fos expression (Lin et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Expression from PRAM was strongly induced by various growth factors known to induce Fos expression.
source: Expression from PRAM was strongly induced by Ca2+ influx (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b) and by various growth factors known to induce Fos expression (Lin et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c and cites Lin et al., 2008.

claim: When expressed in glia, PRAM had minimal basal activity and no activity-dependent induction.
source: When expressed in glia, PRAM had minimal basal activity and no activity-dependent induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: PRAM is a neuron-specific and highly activity-dependent promoter.
source: We concluded that PRAM is a neuron-specific and highly activity-dependent promoter.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results showing PRAM's properties.

claim: The accumulation of tTA outside of the designated experimental window contributed to undesirable background expression of effector genes in the conventional Tet-Off system.
source: Our preliminary evaluation of the conventional Tet-Off system showed that the accumulation of tTA outside of the designated experimental window contributed to the undesirable background expression of effector genes.
evidence: The claim is based on preliminary evaluation of the conventional Tet-Off system.

claim: A destabilized version of tTA (d2tTA) was created by fusing the degradation domain of mouse ornithine decarboxylase (MODC) to the N-terminus of tTA.
source: We therefore created a destabilized version of tTA, d2tTA, by fusing the degradation domain of mouse ornithine decarboxylase (MODC) to the N-terminus of tTA.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and construction of d2tTA.

claim: Using d2tTA led to significantly lower basal expression compared to conventional tTA.
source: Using a luciferase assay after co-transfecting a TRE-luciferase plasmid with either PRAM-tTA or PRAM-d2tTA into cultured neurons, we found that using d2tTA led to significantly lower basal expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e), tighter Dox regulation (Figure 1g), and improved fold induction by a factor of 7–8 compared with conventional tTA (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Using d2tTA led to tighter Dox regulation compared to conventional tTA.
source: Using a luciferase assay after co-transfecting a TRE-luciferase plasmid with either PRAM-tTA or PRAM-d2tTA into cultured neurons, we found that using d2tTA led to significantly lower basal expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e), tighter Dox regulation (Figure 1g), and improved fold induction by a factor of 7–8 compared with conventional tTA (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Using d2tTA improved fold induction by a factor of 7–8 compared with conventional tTA.
source: Using a luciferase assay after co-transfecting a TRE-luciferase plasmid with either PRAM-tTA or PRAM-d2tTA into cultured neurons, we found that using d2tTA led to significantly lower basal expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e), tighter Dox regulation (Figure 1g), and improved fold induction by a factor of 7–8 compared with conventional tTA (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The compact design of the RAM system allows all necessary components to fit within the packaging limit of a single AAV vector (4.9 Kb) with room for an effector gene of up to 1.8 Kb in size.
source: Due to the compact design and small size of PRAM, all the necessary components fit within the packaging limit of a single AAV vector (4.9 Kb) with room for an effector gene of up to 1.8 Kb in size.
evidence: The claim is based on the size calculations of the RAM system components.

claim: Using an optimized titer of AAV-RAM-tdT, close to 100% of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons were infected at DIV7.
source: Using an optimized titer of AAV-RAM-tdT (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a), close to 100% of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons were infected at DIV7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data, with optimization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: With Dox absent throughout, at DIV14 approximately 5% of neurons were labeled with tdT under unstimulated conditions, while nearly 90% of neurons were labeled following bicuculline and 4-aminopyridine stimulation.
source: With Dox absent throughout, at DIV14 approximately 5% of neurons (MAP2-positive cells) were labeled with tdT under unstimulated conditions, while nearly 90% of neurons were labeled following bicuculline (Bic) and 4-aminopyridine (4AP) stimulation (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h–i.

claim: RAM labeling was tightly controlled by Dox, with no labeling cells detected when Dox was present after infection.
source: RAM labeling was tightly controlled by Dox, with no labeling cells detected when Dox was present after infection (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h–i.

claim: No glial cells were tdT positive in the AAV-RAM-tdT cultured neuron experiments.
source: No glial cells were tdT positive (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: With an optimized titer, more than 90% of EGFP+ neurons were also RAM+ after seizure in vivo.
source: With an optimized titer, more than 90% of EGFP+ neurons were also RAM+ after seizure.
evidence: The claim is based on in vivo experimental data with optimized viral titer.

claim: Animals should optimally be off Dox for 24–48 hr before behavioral manipulation for optimal RAM labeling.
source: Using this setup, we found that animals should optimally be off Dox for 24–48 hr before behavioral manipulation (in this case the manipulation was seizure, Figure 2a–d), and that effector gene expression peaked within 24 hr following behavioral manipulation (Figure 2a,e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a–d.

claim: Effector gene expression peaked within 24 hr following behavioral manipulation.
source: Using this setup, we found that animals should optimally be off Dox for 24–48 hr before behavioral manipulation (in this case the manipulation was seizure, Figure 2a–d), and that effector gene expression peaked within 24 hr following behavioral manipulation (Figure 2a,e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,e–g.

claim: Further expression of the effector gene was completely blocked 24 hr after the animals were placed back on Dox chow.
source: In addition, a further expression of the effector gene was completely blocked 24 hr after the animals were placed back on Dox chow (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: RAM labeled a very similar number of DG neurons in animals exposed to Context Only as in those that underwent CFC.
source: We found a significant increase in RAM+ cells in both the CFC and Context Only group, compared to the HC animals (Figure 3c). Importantly, RAM labeled a very similar number of DG neurons in animals exposed to Context Only as in those that underwent CFC (Figure 3c), which is consistent with published studies showing that the hippocampus forms contextual representations independent of shock delivery (Rudy and O'Reilly, 1999; Fanselow, 2000) and that similar levels of IEG induction occur for these two conditions (Ramamoorthi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and is consistent with published studies cited.

claim: The hippocampus forms contextual representations independent of shock delivery.
source: Importantly, RAM labeled a very similar number of DG neurons in animals exposed to Context Only as in those that underwent CFC (Figure 3c), which is consistent with published studies showing that the hippocampus forms contextual representations independent of shock delivery (Rudy and O'Reilly, 1999; Fanselow, 2000) and that similar levels of IEG induction occur for these two conditions (Ramamoorthi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rudy and O'Reilly, 1999 and Fanselow, 2000.

claim: Similar levels of IEG induction occur for CFC and Context Only conditions.
source: Importantly, RAM labeled a very similar number of DG neurons in animals exposed to Context Only as in those that underwent CFC (Figure 3c), which is consistent with published studies showing that the hippocampus forms contextual representations independent of shock delivery (Rudy and O'Reilly, 1999; Fanselow, 2000) and that similar levels of IEG induction occur for these two conditions (Ramamoorthi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ramamoorthi et al., 2011.

claim: The Shock Only condition did not induce RAM activation in the DG.
source: Furthermore, the Shock Only condition did not induce RAM activation at all (Figure 3c), suggesting that RAM labeling was specific to neuronal ensembles involved in contextual learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: RAM labeling was specific to neuronal ensembles involved in contextual learning.
source: Furthermore, the Shock Only condition did not induce RAM activation at all (Figure 3c), suggesting that RAM labeling was specific to neuronal ensembles involved in contextual learning.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that Shock Only did not induce RAM activation.

claim: Learning-specific induction is one of the unique properties of Npas4.
source: Interestingly, such learning-specific induction is one of the unique properties of Npas4 (Ramamoorthi et al., 2011; Sun and Lin, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ramamoorthi et al., 2011 and Sun and Lin, 2016.

claim: Mice that were kept on Dox chow throughout CFC treatment showed a complete lack of RAM+ cells in the DG.
source: Importantly, mice that were kept on Dox chow throughout CFC treatment showed a complete lack of RAM+ cells in the DG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: CFC treatment resulted in RAM+ labeling of 11.4% of infected CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, CFC treatment resulted in RAM+ labeling of 11.4% of infected CA3 pyramidal neurons, compared with 4.4% of infected DG granule cells, similar to published percentages of cells labeled by IEGs in response to CFC in these regions (Kubik et al., 2007; Leutgeb et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with published studies cited.

claim: CFC treatment resulted in RAM+ labeling of 4.4% of infected DG granule cells.
source: Interestingly, CFC treatment resulted in RAM+ labeling of 11.4% of infected CA3 pyramidal neurons, compared with 4.4% of infected DG granule cells, similar to published percentages of cells labeled by IEGs in response to CFC in these regions (Kubik et al., 2007; Leutgeb et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with published studies cited.

claim: RAM labeling persisted for at least 1 week with no noticeable signal loss after CFC.
source: To determine how long expression of the effector gene persists, animals were placed back on Dox 24 hr following CFC, and mKate2 labeling was measured in the following weeks. Labeling persisted for at least 1 week with no noticeable signal loss, began to decay at 2 weeks and was undetectable after 4 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: RAM labeling began to decay at 2 weeks after CFC.
source: Labeling persisted for at least 1 week with no noticeable signal loss, began to decay at 2 weeks and was undetectable after 4 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: RAM labeling was undetectable after 4 weeks following CFC.
source: Labeling persisted for at least 1 week with no noticeable signal loss, began to decay at 2 weeks and was undetectable after 4 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: Ex vivo slice recordings of sparsely RAM+ labeled dentate granule cells 24 hr after CFC revealed that active ensembles could be activated or inhibited by light.
source: To test whether the RAM system drives effector gene expression sufficiently for functional manipulation the following day, we injected AAV-RAM-ChR2 or AAV-RAM-ArchT, which expressed activating channelrhodopsin and inhibiting archeorhodopsin, respectively, into the DG. Ex vivo slice recordings of sparsely RAM+ labeled dentate granule cells 24 hr after CFC revealed that active ensembles could be activated or inhibited by light (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a–j), paving the way for future functional manipulation of neuronal ensembles labeled by the RAM system.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a–j.

claim: Ensembles activated by different contexts can be distinguished within the DG region.
source: Because ensembles activated by different contexts can be distinguished within the DG region (Liu et al., 2012; Garner et al., 2012), and ensembles activated by a particular context are preferentially re-activated following re-exposure to the same context (Barth et al., 2004; Reijmers et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Cruz et al., 2013; Kawashima et al., 2014; Xiu et al., 2014), we chose to focus on active ensembles in the DG following CFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012 and Garner et al., 2012.

claim: Ensembles activated by a particular context are preferentially re-activated following re-exposure to the same context.
source: Because ensembles activated by different contexts can be distinguished within the DG region (Liu et al., 2012; Garner et al., 2012), and ensembles activated by a particular context are preferentially re-activated following re-exposure to the same context (Barth et al., 2004; Reijmers et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Cruz et al., 2013; Kawashima et al., 2014; Xiu et al., 2014), we chose to focus on active ensembles in the DG following CFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mice re-exposed to the conditioning context A froze significantly more than those exposed to the novel context B.
source: Mice re-exposed to the conditioning context A froze significantly more than those exposed to the novel context B, suggesting that mice could distinguish between the two contexts (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The percentage overlap between RAM+ and either FOS+ or NPAS4+ granule cells was significantly higher in animals re-exposed to the same context A than in those subsequently exposed to the new context B.
source: We quantified the degree of overlap between the RAM-labeled and IEG-labeled ensembles. If RAM specifically labels the neuronal ensemble encoding a particular context, we would expect to see more overlap after repeat exposure to the same context than after subsequent exposure to a new context. Indeed, the percentage overlap between RAM+ and either FOS+ or NPAS4+ granule cells (GCs) was significantly higher in animals re-exposed to the same context A than in those subsequently exposed to the new context B (Figure 4c–f,h–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c–f,h–i.

claim: RAM accurately labels neurons that are involved in processing specific context information.
source: Indeed, the percentage overlap between RAM+ and either FOS+ or NPAS4+ granule cells (GCs) was significantly higher in animals re-exposed to the same context A than in those subsequently exposed to the new context B (Figure 4c–f,h–i). This suggests that RAM accurately labels neurons that are involved in processing specific context information.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the overlap data shown in Figure 4c–f,h–i.

claim: The absolute percentage of RAM+ or IEG+ GCs was in the 2–4% range following context exposure.
source: Additionally, the absolute percentage of RAM+ or IEG+ GCs was in the 2–4% range (Figure 4h–i), similar to previous results for this brain region following context exposure (Garner et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h–i and is consistent with published studies cited.

claim: The RAM system labels an active neuronal population similar to that identified by traditional IEG staining.
source: These results indicate that the RAM system labels an active neuronal population similar to that identified by traditional IEG staining.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the overlap data between RAM and IEG labeling.

claim: The overlap percentage between RAM+ and IEG+ GCs for context A-A exposed animals was either on par with or significantly higher than overlap percentages shown in equivalent experiments from previously published studies.
source: Furthermore, the overlap percentage between RAM+ and IEG+ GCs for context A-A exposed animals was either on par with or significantly higher than overlap percentages shown in equivalent experiments from previously published studies.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previously published studies.

claim: The roughly two-fold increase in overlap percentage between context A−A and context A−B exposed animals is on par with previously published studies.
source: Furthermore, the roughly two-fold increase in overlap percentage between context A−A and context A−B exposed animals is also on par with previously published studies (Denny et al., 2014; Ramirez et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previously published studies cited.

claim: TFC led to a dramatic increase in the number of RAM+ neurons in the LA compared to HC controls.
source: Compared to HC controls, TFC led to a dramatic increase in the number of RAM+ neurons in the LA (Figure 5c,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c,f.

claim: Neither Tone nor Shock treatment alone resulted in RAM labeling significantly above the HC level in the LA.
source: Interestingly, neither Tone nor Shock treatment alone resulted in RAM labeling significantly above the HC level (Figure 5c,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c,f.

claim: The relative levels of RAM labeling in LA under each condition were very similar to those of IEG staining reported in published studies.
source: The relative levels of RAM labeling in LA under each condition were very similar to those of IEG staining reported in published studies (Senn et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2003; Radulovic et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with published studies cited.

claim: Long-term synaptic plasticity is known to occur in the LA following TFC to allow the formation of the tone-associated fear memory.
source: Furthermore, long-term synaptic plasticity is known to occur in the LA following TFC to allow the formation of the tone-associated fear memory, while tone or shock alone does not result in long-term behavioral or synaptic changes (Rogan et al., 1997; Rogan and LeDoux, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rogan et al., 1997 and Rogan and LeDoux, 1995.

claim: Tone or shock alone does not result in long-term behavioral or synaptic changes in the LA.
source: Furthermore, long-term synaptic plasticity is known to occur in the LA following TFC to allow the formation of the tone-associated fear memory, while tone or shock alone does not result in long-term behavioral or synaptic changes (Rogan et al., 1997; Rogan and LeDoux, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rogan et al., 1997 and Rogan and LeDoux, 1995.

claim: The neuronal ensembles labeled by RAM in the LA are likely involved in fear memory formation.
source: Our result (Figure 5c,f) therefore suggests that the neuronal ensembles labeled by RAM are likely involved in fear memory formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the RAM labeling pattern and known properties of LA plasticity.

claim: TFC greatly increased the number of RAM labeled neurons in the BA, compared to HC.
source: Like in the LA, TFC greatly increased the number of RAM labeled neurons in the BA, compared to HC (Figure 5e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e–f.

claim: The numbers of RAM labeled neurons in both Tone and Shock groups in the BA, although significantly lower than in the TFC group, were much greater than in HC.
source: In addition, the numbers of RAM labeled neurons in both Tone and Shock groups, although significantly lower than in the TFC group, were much greater than in HC (Figure 5e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e–f.

claim: The relative levels of RAM labeling in BA were in agreement with those of IEG expression previously reported under similar conditions.
source: Again, the relative levels of RAM labeling in BA were in agreement with those of IEG expression previously reported under similar conditions (Senn et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2003; Radulovic et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with published studies cited.

claim: In animals subjected to TFC, the neuronal ensembles labeled by RAM in the CeA were significantly larger compared to HC.
source: In animals subjected to TFC, the neuronal ensembles labeled by RAM in the CeA were significantly larger compared to HC (Figure 5g–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5g–i.

claim: RAM can label neuronal ensembles that are important for fear memory formation in the amygdala.
source: Taken together, these results indicated RAM can label neuronal ensembles that are important for fear memory formation in the amygdala.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the RAM labeling patterns in LA, BA, and CeA.

claim: A significantly higher percentage of RAM+ labeling was observed in animals subjected to IS compared to HC controls in the rat mPFC.
source: Five days after injection, rats were taken off Dox for four days before being subjected to the inescapable stress (IS) paradigm, which is known to engage the mPFC (Wang et al., 2014). A significantly higher percentage of RAM+ labeling was observed in animals subjected to IS compared to HC controls (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c–d and cites Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The RAM system can be used successfully in species other than mouse.
source: These results indicate that the RAM system can be used successfully in species other than mouse, and also in an additional brain region (the mPFC).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on successful application in rats.

claim: Drosophila contains both Fos− and Npas4-like transcription factors.
source: Since Drosophila contains both Fos− and Npas4-like transcription factors (Perkins et al., 1988; Jiang and Crews, 2007), we tested PRAM in flies using a strategy that has been successfully implemented for CRE-based reporters (Zhang et al., 2015; Tanenhaus et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Perkins et al., 1988 and Jiang and Crews, 2007.

claim: RAM-luc reporter activity was circadian in adult Drosophila brain.
source: Luciferase activity measured in live flies over time showed high expression in the adult Drosophila brain. Most importantly, RAM-luc reporter activity was circadian (Figure 6g), suggesting that PRAM functions as a robust activity-dependent promoter in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: PRAM functions as a robust activity-dependent promoter in Drosophila.
source: Most importantly, RAM-luc reporter activity was circadian (Figure 6g), suggesting that PRAM functions as a robust activity-dependent promoter in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the circadian activity of RAM-luc shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Two days after training, RAM-luc activity in FS-trained flies was significantly higher than in those in the control group exposed to un-paired odor and shock presentation (BS training).
source: Two days after training, RAM-luc activity in FS-trained flies was significantly higher than in those in the control group exposed to un-paired odor and shock presentation (Backward Spaced, or BS, training; Figure 6h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The RAM-luc reporter fly can be used to identify memory-specific cellular populations in Drosophila.
source: Although further work is needed to completely validate the RAM-luc reporter fly in behavioral studies, these results suggest that it can be used to identify memory-specific cellular populations in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the preliminary data from the olfactory memory task.

claim: The number of GAD67-labeled GABAergic neurons that were RAM+ was significantly higher in animals subjected to IS than the HC controls in rat mPFC.
source: We injected rats with AAV-RAM-NLS-mKate2 and AAV-Ef1α-EGFP into mPFC and subjected the animals to the IS paradigm (Figure 7a–b). Indeed, we found that the number of GAD67-labeled GABAergic neurons that were RAM+ was significantly higher in animals subjected to IS than the HC controls (Figure 7c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c–d.

claim: A small fraction of the induced RAM+ GABAergic neurons were parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons.
source: A small fraction of these induced RAM+ GABAergic neurons were parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: CFC treatment resulted in RAM labeling in a substantial number of somatostatin-positive GABAergic neurons in the hilus of the DG in mice.
source: In mice, CFC treatment resulted in RAM labeling in a substantial number of somatostatin-positive GABAergic neurons in the hilus of the DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–f.

claim: PRAM was induced by KCl stimulation in cultured cortical neurons derived from Gad2-Cre mice.
source: Additionally, using the Cre-dependent FLEX system and luciferase assay, we confirmed that PRAM was induced by KCl stimulation in cultured cortical neurons derived from Gad2-Cre mice wherein Cre is expressed exclusively in neurons expressing the GABAergic neuron marker Gad65 (Figure 7e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e–g.

claim: The RAM system achieves robust activity-dependent labeling of GABAergic neurons.
source: These results confirm that the RAM system achieves robust activity-dependent labeling of GABAergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on multiple experiments showing RAM labeling in GABAergic neurons.

claim: When CRAM-tdT virus was injected into the DG of Gad2-Cre mice, only GABAergic neurons (most prominently somatostatin-expressing neurons in the hilus) and none of the glutamatergic granule cells were labeled with tdT after kainic acid-induced seizure.
source: When CRAM-tdT virus was injected into the DG of Gad2-Cre mice, only GABAergic neurons (most prominently somatostatin-expressing neurons in the hilus) and none of the glutamatergic granule cells were labeled with tdT after kainic acid-induced seizure (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3a–d.

claim: IEGs are known to be induced by experience in GABAergic neurons.
source: While IEGs are known to be induced by experience in GABAergic neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014), active ensembles of GABAergic neurons have not been explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: Active ensembles of GABAergic neurons have not been explored.
source: While IEGs are known to be induced by experience in GABAergic neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014), active ensembles of GABAergic neurons have not been explored.

claim: Significantly more tdT-labeled neurons were observed in animals subjected to IS compared to HC controls when using CRAM to label DMS-projecting mPFC neurons in rats.
source: Since a major projection of the rat PFC is the dorsal striatum (Gabbott et al., 2005), we injected a retrograde canine adenovirus that expresses Cre recombinase into the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) to deliver Cre to DMS-projecting mPFC neurons. AAV-CRAM-tdT was subsequently injected into the mPFC and the animals were subjected to IS treatment (Figure 7i–j). We observed significantly more tdT-labeled neurons in animals subjected to IS compared to HC controls (Figure 7k–l), suggesting CRAM successfully labeled IS-activated mPFC neuronal ensembles that project to the DMS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7k–l and cites Gabbott et al., 2005.

claim: CRAM successfully labeled IS-activated mPFC neuronal ensembles that project to the DMS.
source: We observed significantly more tdT-labeled neurons in animals subjected to IS compared to HC controls (Figure 7k–l), suggesting CRAM successfully labeled IS-activated mPFC neuronal ensembles that project to the DMS.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7k–l.

claim: The RAM system delivers unprecedented versatility and much improved selectivity compared to existing methods used to gain access to recently active neuronal ensembles.
source: Here we present the RAM (Robust Activity Marking) system, which makes possible the sensitive and specific labeling and manipulation of the active ensembles of neurons associated with a designated sensory and behavioral experience. Compared to existing methods used to gain access to recently active neuronal ensembles (Guenthner et al., 2013; Reijmers et al., 2007; Smeyne et al., 1992; Eguchi and Yamaguchi, 2009; Kawashima et al., 2013), the RAM system delivers unprecedented versatility and much improved selectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with existing methods cited.

claim: In vivo RAM achieved 37-fold and five-fold increases in labeling after CFC, compared to HC controls, in CA3 and DG, respectively.
source: In vivo RAM achieved 37-fold and five-fold increases in labeling after CFC, compared to HC controls, in CA3 and DG, respectively. This is significantly greater than the two–three-fold induction achieved using existing technologies (Guenthner et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and comparison with existing technologies cited.

claim: Existing technologies achieve two–three-fold induction in labeling after CFC.
source: This is significantly greater than the two–three-fold induction achieved using existing technologies (Guenthner et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to Guenthner et al., 2013 and Ramirez et al., 2013.

claim: The five–37-fold induction achieved with the RAM system implies that 80–97% of the labeled neurons are truly associated with the specific experience.
source: The five–37-fold induction achieved with the RAM system implies that 80–97% of the labeled neurons are truly associated with the specific experience, compared to 50–67% with existing technologies, representing a dramatic improvement in signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the fold induction data.

claim: With existing technologies, 50–67% of the labeled neurons are truly associated with the specific experience.
source: The five–37-fold induction achieved with the RAM system implies that 80–97% of the labeled neurons are truly associated with the specific experience, compared to 50–67% with existing technologies, representing a dramatic improvement in signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the fold induction of existing technologies.

claim: After pentylenetetrazol (PTZ)-induced seizure, only about 20% of the PV+ neurons, compared to over 80% of somatostatin expressing (SST+) neurons, in the cortex were transcriptionally activated to express FOS.
source: For example, activated PV+ neurons appear to be less likely to express IEGs. Even after pentylenetetrazol (PTZ)-induced seizure, only about 20% of the PV+ neurons, compared to over 80% of somatostatin expressing (SST+) neurons, in the cortex were transcriptionally activated to express FOS (Figure 7—figure supplement 4a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4a–b.

claim: A similar trend of lower IEG expression in PV+ neurons compared to SST+ neurons was observed in DG after KA-induced seizure.
source: A similar trend was observed in DG after KA-induced seizure (Figure 7—figure supplement 4a, c), suggesting either PV+ neurons may be less likely to be recruited to active ensembles or they may require non-IEG-based approaches to be effectively labeled.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4a, c.

claim: PV+ neurons may be less likely to be recruited to active ensembles or they may require non-IEG-based approaches to be effectively labeled.
source: A similar trend was observed in DG after KA-induced seizure (Figure 7—figure supplement 4a, c), suggesting either PV+ neurons may be less likely to be recruited to active ensembles or they may require non-IEG-based approaches to be effectively labeled.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observation of lower IEG expression in PV+ neurons.

source: The compact design of the RAM system allows it to be packaged into a single AAV while still accommodating an effector gene up to 1.8 Kb in size.
evidence: The claim is based on the size calculations of the RAM system components.

source: The RAM system can readily accommodate most of the effector genes commonly used to label or manipulate neural circuits.

claim: In cases where other, larger promoters and/or larger effector genes are needed, the RAM system can split between two AAVs.
source: In cases where other, larger promoters and/or larger effector genes are needed, the RAM system can split between two AAVs, one containing the d2tTA expression cassette and the other the TRE-effector cassette.
evidence: The claim describes a potential modification of the RAM system for larger constructs.
